target.title: feat(google): gate Gemini CLI runtime harness behind explicit opt-in
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a Google provider compatibility problem where the bundled Google plugin exposes the Gemini CLI harness through direct runtime plugin registration by default, even though the supported default Google model path should remain the API-backed `google` provider.

The affected workflow is Google provider setup/runtime selection. This PR keeps existing setup-registry `google-gemini-cli` backend compatibility available while requiring explicit operator opt-in for direct bundled runtime registration of the Gemini CLI provider/backend.

## Why This Change Was Made

The change makes the Google provider boundary explicit: `google` remains the API-backed Google AI Studio/Gemini provider, `google-vertex` remains the Vertex provider, and `google-gemini-cli` is treated as an optional local CLI harness.

The opt-in is controlled by `OPENCLAW_ENABLE_GOOGLE_GEMINI_CLI_HARNESS=1`. This applies only to direct bundled runtime plugin registration. The setup-registry default for `google-gemini-cli` remains available so existing setup-only backend resolution continues to work.

The PR also aligns manifest metadata, onboarding copy, provider contract copy, public Google provider docs, and docs navigation with that compatibility policy.

## User Impact

Users configuring the default Google provider continue to see the API-backed Google path instead of being directed toward Gemini CLI OAuth by default.

Existing `google-gemini-cli` setup/backend resolution remains available through the setup-registry compatibility path. Operators who want direct bundled runtime registration of the Gemini CLI provider/backend can set `OPENCLAW_ENABLE_GOOGLE_GEMINI_CLI_HARNESS=1`.

target.title: fix(telegram): webhook updates survive crashes and restarts via durable spooling
target.body:
Closes #98777

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Telegram webhook mode silently and permanently lost updates: the handler acked 200 to Telegram before any persistence, so a gateway crash, restart, deploy, or even a transient processing failure (DB lock, provider error) during an in-flight update dropped it forever — Telegram saw the 200 and never redelivers. Three sibling webhook-mode gaps are fixed with it: a single transient network blip during startup `getMe` failed the whole account start (burning the supervisor's cumulative restart budget), the webhook bot's HTTP transport was never closed (leaking keep-alive sockets on every restart — the same class as #68128, fixed for polling only), and the generic 120 req/min pre-auth rate limit throttled Telegram's own authenticated delivery on busy bots, growing `pending_update_count` until Telegram dropped old updates.

## Why This Change Was Made

Webhook mode now uses the same durability model as polling: the parsed update is written to the SQLite ingress spool **before** the 200 ack (a spool write failure returns non-200 so Telegram redelivers — that is the contract), and a webhook drain replays spooled updates through the bot with per-lane ordering, claim refresh, capped exponential backoff, and age-gated dead-lettering, including recovery of leftover updates on startup. Enqueue-time duplicate detection makes Telegram's own webhook retries idempotent. Rather than duplicating polling's retry policy, it is extracted into a shared `spooled-update-retry-policy.ts` consumed by both drains — including the age-gate semantics from 55d31beeef0 (over-limit updates keep retrying at the 3-minute cap and only tombstone once 24h old), now applied to webhook too. Startup `bot.init()` retries transient errors with the existing webhook retry classifier (401 stays fatal); the webhook owns its transport and closes it exactly once on shutdown and on startup failure (evicted probe-cache transports are closed as well); and the request path validates the Telegram secret first, so only failed secret guesses consume the abuse rate-limit budget — the pinned security contracts (constant-time compare, single-header enforcement, connection close on 401, body-size limits) are unchanged.

## User Impact

Webhook-mode Telegram accounts no longer lose messages across restarts, deploys, or transient failures — updates survive durably and replay, matching polling-mode reliability. Accounts come up cleanly after reboots instead of dying on the first network blip, long-running gateways stop leaking sockets on webhook restarts, and busy bots no longer have their own traffic rate-limited into growing delivery backlogs.

## Evidence

- New regression tests (`webhook.test.ts`, +313 lines): update spooled before ack and redelivered after a transient processing failure; non-200 when the spool write fails; leftover spooled updates drained on startup; young over-limit updates stay pending while >24h-old ones dead-letter (age-gate parity); transient `getMe` then success starts the account while 401 stays fatal; transport closed exactly once on shutdown and startup failure (plus `probe.test.ts` for evicted transports); authenticated request storm passes while unauthenticated storm still 429s.
- Extraction proof: `extensions/telegram/src/polling-session.test.ts` is **unchanged from `main`** and passes against the shared policy module — polling behavior is identical by its own tests, including the age-gate tests from 55d31beeef0.
- Validation on this branch rebased onto current `main`: `pnpm tsgo:extensions` pass; `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` on `webhook.test.ts`, `probe.test.ts`, `polling-session.test.ts` — 114 tests pass; `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on touched files clean; repo autoreview (branch mode vs `origin/main`) clean.

target.title: feat(mxc): add Windows MXC sandbox backend
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw does not currently have an official installable MXC sandbox backend for Windows hosts that can run sandboxed commands through Microsoft eXecution Containers. This leaves MXC-capable Windows environments without a first-party plugin path for ProcessContainer-backed execution and filesystem bridge operations.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an official OpenShell-style external `mxc` sandbox plugin package (`@openclaw/mxc-sandbox`) with Windows-only readiness checks, plugin-owned MXC SDK dependency ownership, ProcessContainer payload construction, a plugin-side launcher, host-backed filesystem bridge support, sandbox policy loading, and targeted tests.

The plugin source lives under `extensions/mxc`, but it is packaged as an installable plugin (`bundledDist: false`) so the MXC SDK/native dependency is owned by the plugin package instead of an unshipped bundled `node_modules` tree. The backend uses the stable current MXC `0.7.0-alpha` schema and keeps sandbox defaults conservative: curated environments, headless UI, per-exec temp directories, absolute binary overrides, host-derived Windows roots, read-only default workspace access for `none`/`ro`, and fail-closed unsupported policy handling.

## User Impact

Users on MXC-capable Windows hosts can install the official MXC sandbox plugin, restart the Gateway, configure `sandbox.backend: "mxc"`, and run OpenClaw sandboxed commands through MXC. Non-Windows or unsupported Windows hosts remain unaffected because the plugin stays dormant when readiness probes fail.

Install command:

```bash
openclaw plugins install @openclaw/mxc-sandbox
```

## Evidence

- `pnpm test:extension mxc -- --reporter=verbose` — passed.
- `pnpm test extensions\mxc test\scripts\generate-npm-shrinkwrap.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose` — passed.
- `pnpm test:changed` — passed.
- `pnpm release:plugins:npm:check -- --plugins @openclaw/mxc-sandbox` — passed; publishable plugin metadata looks OK.
- `pnpm release:plugins:clawhub:check -- --plugins @openclaw/mxc-sandbox` — passed; publishable plugin metadata looks OK.

target.title: feat: add durable routines registry
target.body:
Closes #98515

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw has cron jobs, tasks, heartbeat, commitments, and channel/session delivery primitives, but no first-class durable registry for recurring team-operations routines. Operators can schedule work today, but they cannot create, inspect, pause, delete, or recover a typed routine as one durable product object with ownership, delivery target, run status, and replay-safe mutation semantics.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds the smallest complete routine slice: a typed routine registry backed by the shared SQLite state DB, Gateway RPC methods, CLI entrypoints, and a schedule trigger that delegates execution to the canonical cron service rather than creating a second scheduler. The design keeps cron as the scheduler owner and routines as the durable registry owner, with internal create/toggle stages so retries recover safely after partial persistence or scheduler failures.

Non-goals for this draft: no Control UI yet, no channel-watch/repository-event/webhook triggers yet, no duplicate scheduler, and no transcript attachment. The trigger model is shaped so those future triggers can share the same routine subsystem instead of growing a second path.

AI-assisted implementation and review were used for this draft PR.

## User Impact

Users and operators can now use `openclaw routines` or Gateway RPC to create, list, inspect, enable, disable, and delete durable scheduled routines. Routine inspection shows owner, delivery target, enabled/deleted state, last and next run visibility, status, and last error context. Repeated create/toggle/delete calls are idempotent, and restart/replay behavior preserves the intended routine state instead of silently losing a schedule toggle or rolling scheduler state backward.

target.title: fix(macos): preserve profile env in launch agent
target.body:
Fixes #98594.

## What Problem This Solves

The macOS app launch-at-login plist only preserved `PATH` in `EnvironmentVariables`. If a user enabled Launch at login while running OpenClaw with a custom profile, the login-launched app lost `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` and fell back to the default `~/.openclaw/openclaw.json` profile.

## Why This Change Was Made

`OpenClawPaths` already treats `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR` and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` as the supported profile-selection contract. The app LaunchAgent now carries those two non-empty environment variables alongside `PATH` so the next login uses the same profile that was active when autostart was enabled.

The plist is generated through `PropertyListSerialization` instead of a hand-written XML string, so paths containing XML-sensitive characters are escaped by Foundation.

## User Impact

macOS users with custom OpenClaw profiles can enable Launch at login without silently switching back to the default profile on the next login.

## Evidence

- Added focused Swift coverage for:
  - preserving non-empty `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` and `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`
  - omitting blank profile env values
  - parsing the generated plist after XML-sensitive profile paths
- `git diff --cached --check` passed before commit.
- `swiftc -parse apps/macos/Sources/OpenClaw/LaunchAgentManager.swift` passed locally.

target.title: feat(feishu): add segment streaming mode
target.body:
## Summary

Add an opt-in Feishu streaming delivery mode that accumulates model output and flushes complete segments at pause points, without changing the existing CardKit streaming-card default.

## Motivation

Feishu currently uses `channels.feishu.streaming` for CardKit live streaming. That behavior is useful when users want one live card that updates as the model generates text.

Some workflows need a different delivery style: show completed model text before a tool call, keep tool/status output in order, and then send the follow-up answer after the model resumes. Sending these boundaries as complete segments avoids sentence-by-sentence card updates while still giving users useful progress before the final reply.

## Configuration Behavior

`streaming` remains the top-level enable/disable switch for Feishu streaming delivery. `streamingMode` only applies when `streaming` is enabled.

| `streaming` | `streamingMode` | Behavior                                                                                                                                                |
| ----------- | --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `false`     | `"card"`        | Streaming is disabled. Feishu sends replies through the regular non-streaming path; the mode value is ignored.                                          |
| `false`     | `"segment"`     | Streaming is disabled. Partial text is not accumulated and pause-point segment flushing is not enabled; the mode value is ignored.                      |
| `true`      | `"card"`        | Existing CardKit streaming behavior. Feishu updates one live card and closes it with the final content. This remains the default.                       |
| `true`      | `"segment"`     | New pause-point segment behavior. Feishu accumulates partial text and sends complete segments on tool start, idle, block, tool payload, or final reply. |

`chunkMode` still applies after a reply or segment is ready to send. In segment mode, `streamingMode: "segment"` decides when to flush a semantic segment, then `chunkMode` decides whether that segment needs to be split by length or newline before sending to Feishu.

## Changes

- Add `channels.feishu.streamingMode` with supported values:
  - `"card"`: default, existing CardKit streaming behavior
  - `"segment"`: accumulate model text and flush at pause points
- Preserve current `channels.feishu.streaming` semantics:
  - `true` enables streaming delivery
  - `false` disables streaming delivery
  - default mode remains CardKit streaming
- In segment mode:
  - partial model output is accumulated
  - accumulated text is flushed on tool start, idle, block, tool payload, or final reply
  - duplicate final text after an idle flush is suppressed
  - segment sends are serialized so final/tool payloads cannot overtake an in-flight partial flush
  - each flushed segment independently uses `renderMode: "auto"`
  - mentions are attached only to the first text segment
  - reasoning preview callbacks stay disabled because segment mode does not use live cards
- Update Feishu config schema, generated config metadata, docs, and tests.

## Example

Use segment delivery with:

```json5
{
  channels: {
    feishu: {
      streaming: true,
      streamingMode: "segment",
    },
  },
}
```

Default behavior remains:

```json5
{
  channels: {
    feishu: {
      streaming: true,
      streamingMode: "card",
    },
  },
}
```

## Compatibility

- Existing configs that only set `channels.feishu.streaming` keep the same behavior because `streamingMode` defaults to `"card"`.
- `streaming: false` continues to disable streaming delivery regardless of `streamingMode`.
- Segment mode is opt-in and does not change CardKit streaming-card behavior.

## Real behavior proof

- Behavior or issue addressed: Feishu configs can opt into `streamingMode: "segment"`, and the dispatcher sends one completed segment before a tool pause and a second completed segment after the tool returns.
- Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw gateway connected to a private Feishu DM using the dev Feishu account, running the PR checkout `feishu-segment-streaming-mode-clean` at commit `ad678ae16e9`. Node.js `v22.22.2`; pnpm dependencies installed in `/root/.openclaw/workspace-dev/projects/fork-repos/openclaw`.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch: Sent this Feishu DM to the dev agent: `First reply with exactly one line: segment-one-ok. Then you must call a tool to check the current date or time. After the tool returns, reply with exactly one line: segment-two-ok.` The dev Feishu account was configured with `streaming: true` and `streamingMode: "segment"`.
- Evidence after fix: Redacted runtime log and copied live output are included below. Gateway journal shows `segment flush reason=toolStart` followed by `segment flush reason=final`; agent session output shows `segment-one-ok`, `toolCall: session_status`, and `segment-two-ok`.
- Observed result after fix: The live Feishu turn emitted `segment-one-ok`, paused for the `session_status` tool call, then emitted `segment-two-ok`. Gateway logs show two segment flushes for the same Feishu turn, first with `reason=toolStart` and then with `reason=final`, and the dispatch completed with `replies=2`.
- What was not tested: Broad multi-user/load behavior and media upload fallback in a real Feishu tenant were not tested in this live run; media fallback behavior is covered by the targeted Feishu dispatcher tests below.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): Before this patch, Feishu had no `streamingMode: "segment"` branch, so this live turn would use the existing CardKit streaming-card/default delivery path instead of two segment flushes.

Copied and redacted gateway journal plus agent-session output from the live Feishu run:

target.title: fix(gateway): render codex inline media once
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: Codex-harness replies that emitted local `MEDIA:` image directives could fail to become trusted outgoing media, leaving inline images text-only or unavailable to WebChat/Control UI.
- Why it matters: Agents using the Codex harness should be able to return generated/local images inline without requiring channel-specific manual workarounds, and users should not see duplicate assistant turns for one image reply.
- What changed: Trust structured local media markers from non-external tool results, while preserving the existing registered-tool trust checks; replace the latest raw assistant `MEDIA:` transcript turn with the normalized media-bearing message instead of appending a second assistant image turn.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): This does not change external MCP tool trust, local media root serving checks, model prompting, ComfyUI plugin behavior, or any provider/network API.

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all touched areas)

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [x] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [x] API / contracts
- [x] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

No matching upstream issue was found. Searches checked: `inline image`, `inline media`, `Codex harness image`, `MEDIA: image`, `assistant-media`, `managed media`, `Control UI image`, and duplicate image/WebChat terms.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

- Root cause: The Codex/AppServer path can persist the model-authored assistant reply as raw text containing `MEDIA:<local path>` while the gateway reply payload carries the parsed/normalized media URL. The WebChat transcript bridge treated those as separate assistant replies and appended the normalized media message after the raw directive turn.

target.title: fix(gateway): distinguish reachable gateway from failed status probe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw gateway status` prints `Warm-up: launch agents can take a few seconds. Try again shortly.` whenever the RPC probe fails while the managed service is loaded and running — even when the gateway process is up and owns its port and the probe is failing for an unrelated reason such as a wrong probe auth token or bad config.

In that state the gateway is clearly not "warming up", so telling the operator to wait and retry is the wrong nudge — they should be checking the probe credentials/config (or restarting if the gateway is wedged). This follows the same status-distinction lineage as the recent `/status` slices (#97479, #97878).

## Why This Change Was Made

Deep status already computes `status.health.healthy`, which is `running && owns-the-listening-port` (it is not a reachability proof). When that is true and the RPC probe still fails, it is an unambiguous "not warm-up" signal, so the message changes from warm-up to recovery guidance. Everything else keeps the existing warm-up message:

- `health.healthy === true`: the gateway process is running and owns the port, so a failed probe is not a warm-up delay. The cause is probe credentials/config or a wedged gateway (a wedged gateway that still owns the port is also reported as `healthy === true`), so we point the operator at both paths without asserting a single cause.
- otherwise: keep the existing warm-up message. `health.healthy === false` is deliberately not redirected — it is ambiguous (a just-started gateway reports `false` until it binds the port; the port may be held by a foreign process; or a stale gateway PID may own it), and those cases are already covered by the dedicated stale-PID, "port not listening", and port-conflict diagnostics elsewhere in the status output. Unknown health (shallow status) also keeps warm-up.

This is presentation-only. Health computation, probe behavior, service-manager behavior, config, and RPC are untouched; no new config/default surfaces, no new imports.

## User Impact

When the RPC probe fails on a running service whose gateway owns the port, `openclaw gateway status` now prints:

> Gateway process is running and owns the gateway port, so this is not a warm-up delay. Check the probe credentials/config, or restart the gateway and inspect its logs if it stays unresponsive.

instead of the generic warm-up line. All other states (gateway still starting up, port held by another process, stale PID, or unknown health) keep the existing warm-up message and the existing dedicated diagnostics. No behavior change beyond the printed guidance text.

## Evidence

- Focused render tests — `pnpm test src/cli/daemon-cli/status.print.test.ts` → 20 passed (17 existing + 3 new):
  - `health.healthy:true` + failed probe + running → owns-port "not a warm-up delay" guidance, no warm-up line.
  - `health.healthy:false` + port busy + running → warm-up line preserved, no "Gateway process is …" guidance (guards against misfiring restart guidance on a foreign port conflict).
  - no `health` → existing warm-up line preserved, no "Gateway process is …" line.
- Typecheck: `pnpm tsgo:core` and `pnpm tsgo:test:src` clean. Format: `oxfmt --check` clean.
- Render-path capture — invoked the real `printDaemonStatus` (no mocks; real CLI status styles, real `formatCliCommand`, real runtime) with a constructed `DaemonStatus` per case. This exercises the changed render path, not gather/deep status (which is unchanged). Excerpted output (surrounding status lines omitted):

```
########## health.healthy=true + port busy (running, owns port, probe failed) ##########
Runtime: running (pid 8000)
Gateway process is running and owns the gateway port, so this is not a warm-up delay. Check the probe credentials/config, or restart the gateway and inspect its logs if it stays unresponsive.
Connectivity probe: failed
  gateway closed (1008 policy violation: invalid token)

########## health.healthy=false + port busy (unhealthy/ambiguous) ##########
Runtime: running (pid 8000)
Warm-up: launch agents can take a few seconds. Try again shortly.

########## health=undefined + port busy (shallow status, unknown) ##########
Runtime: running (pid 8000)
Warm-up: launch agents can take a few seconds. Try again shortly.
```

target.title: fix(agents): use CJK-aware token estimation for tool results
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves
`TOOL_RESULT_CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 2` 与 `estimateStringChars`的中文字符权重(4 chars/token)不匹配，导致CJK-rich内容被2倍高估，触发false token overflow错误，中断中文工作流。

例如：85k中文字符被估计为170k tokens，实际应为~85k，导致本不应触发的preemptive compaction提前激活。

## Evidence
### Verifiable Behavior
- **Issue Reference**: #95327
- **Test Results**:
```
[pnpm test] preemptive-compaction.test.ts
Tests 21 passed (21)
Duration 6.03s

CJK Text Test: 85,000+ Chinese chars estimated as ~85,000 tokens (ratio: ~1.0)
CJK Tool Result Test: 80k CJK chars fit within 128k budget with 20k reserve
Mixed Lang Test: ratio 0.8-1.5, healthy
JSON Payload Test: CJK-heavy JSON tool result no longer triggers false overflow
Non-serializable Test: circular non-array content completes precheck without throwing
```

### Real Behavior Proof
Below is the terminal output from running a standalone script against this PR branch. The script exercises the actual production estimation helpers (`estimateLlmBoundaryTokenPressure` and `shouldPreemptivelyCompactBeforePrompt`) with realistic CJK-heavy, mixed, and Latin-only tool-result payloads.

Command: `pnpm exec tsx .tmp-cjk-proof.ts`

```
=== PR #95447 real-behavior proof: CJK-aware tool-result token estimation ===

--- 85k CJK-heavy tool result ---
  Input chars:              85,000
  CJK ratio:                90.0%
  Adjusted char weight:     314,500 (CJK-aware)
  Before-fix token estimate: 165,173  (/2 ratio)
  After-fix token estimate:  94,421  (CJK-aware)
  After-fix route:          fits
  After-fix overflow:       0 tokens

--- Mixed CJK + Latin tool result (CJK majority) ---
  Input chars:              49,000
  CJK ratio:                61.2%
  Adjusted char weight:     139,000 (CJK-aware)
  Before-fix token estimate: 73,035  (/2 ratio)
  After-fix token estimate:  41,771  (CJK-aware)
  After-fix route:          fits
  After-fix overflow:       0 tokens

--- Latin-only tool result ---
  Input chars:              67,000
  CJK ratio:                0.0%
  Adjusted char weight:     67,000 (CJK-aware)
  Before-fix token estimate: 35,235  (/2 ratio)
  After-fix token estimate:  40,271  (CJK-aware)
  After-fix route:          compact_then_truncate
  After-fix overflow:       13,271 tokens

=== Result ===
CJK-heavy tool results no longer trigger false overflow;
non-CJK tool results keep the existing conservative estimate.
```

The proof shows that a 85k-character CJK-heavy tool result was previously estimated at ~165k tokens (false overflow → would route to `compact_only`) and is now estimated at ~94k tokens (fits within a 128k budget with 20k reserve → routes to `fits`). The Latin-only case still uses the conservative `/2` ratio and correctly routes to compaction when it genuinely overflows.

### Technical Evidence
- **Before**: `TOOL_RESULT_CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 2` 导致CJK被double-count
- **After**:
  - CJK比例≥50%时使用`ESTIMATED_CHARS_PER_TOKEN = 4`，与正常文本估计一致
  - 非CJK场景保持保守`/2`比例
  - JSON tool-result payload 和 unknown record fallback 现在也被纳入 CJK ratio 采样
  - ratio pre-pass 使用与 token-pressure 估算相同的 `safeJsonStringify` fallback，避免非序列化内容抛出
- **Files Changed**:
  - `src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/preemptive-compaction.ts`
  - `src/utils/cjk-chars.ts`
- **Test Updates**: `preemptive-compaction.test.ts` 增加 5 个 CJK/JSON/fallback 相关测试用例

### Regression Risk
- Low: 仅修改 tool-result token 估算路径，非 CJK 场景保持原有保守行为
- 所有 21 个估计测试通过
- 新增非序列化内容回归测试，确保 precheck 不会因 `JSON.stringify` 失败而中断 turn

## Why This Change Was Made
使 tool result token estimation 与 CJK 字符权重对齐，防止 false overflow，确保多语言工作流公平对待 CJK 字符；同时覆盖 JSON/unknown payload 和安全 fallback，避免 estimator 分支遗漏。

## User Impact
- 中文工作流不再因错误的 token overflow 中断
- Tool result 上下文预算更准确（含结构化 JSON 返回）
- 无配置或操作变更，零用户学习成本

target.title: fix #95295: [Bug]: Web UI sidebar hides existing child-spawned subagent sessions across agent scopes
target.body:
## Summary

- Problem: The Web UI sidebar Recent Sessions list could hide existing child-spawned subagent transcripts when the current chat scope was another agent, so users could not intentionally rediscover those sessions from the left sidebar.
- Solution: Keep the existing scoped/default behavior, but add an explicit sidebar **All agents** mode for sidebar-owned refreshes only. Checkpoint entry and Sessions-tab mutation refreshes stay scoped to the session's agent.
- What changed: Added sidebar state and UI for the scope toggle, made sidebar-owned requests omit scoped `agentId`, kept cron/global/unknown/archived rows excluded, and added follow-up regressions so All agents cannot leak into checkpoint opener, checkpoint branch/restore, post-send, terminal-final, or deferred session-message refreshes.
- What did NOT change / out of scope: This does not change the chat picker, default sidebar scoping, shared `loadSessions` explicit `agentId` semantics, gateway protocol schema, stored transcript format, migration behavior, public config, or default visibility of subagent/spawned sessions. Making All agents a global Sessions-tab mode is intentionally out of scope.
- Why it matters / User impact: Users with persisted child-spawned subagent work can intentionally find and reopen those existing transcripts from the sidebar without losing the safer scoped default view, and checkpoint/Sessions-tab actions no longer inherit that wider sidebar-only visibility.
- Fixes #95295

## What Problem This Solves

The sidebar needed an intentional way to rediscover persisted child-spawned subagent sessions across agent scopes, but earlier passes made the sidebar All agents state too easy to reuse outside the sidebar boundary. In particular, opening checkpoint recovery from chat, checkpoint branch/restore actions, post-send reloads, terminal-final reloads, and deferred `session.message` reloads could refresh shared `sessionsResult` without an agent scope after All agents was enabled. This update keeps the opt-in sidebar behavior while deriving non-sidebar refresh scope from the current/checkpoint/target session key itself, so Sessions-tab, checkpoint, chat-send, terminal, and deferred message refreshes remain scoped.

## Evidence

- Focused checkpoint opener, branch/restore, post-send, terminal-final, and deferred session-message regressions, requested UI test set, UI CI-failure regression subset, core/core-test TypeScript checks, test-type checks, oxlint, and whitespace checks all passed locally after the follow-up scope repair and CI mock/import repair.
- Existing UI/session-store proof from the prior revision still applies for the sidebar All agents behavior: scoped main results omit the orchestrator child, unscoped All agents results include the child-spawned row with canonical `spawnedBy`, and Chrome showed the subagent row only after pressing **All agents**.
- Proof gap: I still cannot run a long-lived live gateway/Mantis proof in this contributor environment. The local proof uses focused repository tests plus the existing deterministic Control UI/session-store browser proof; it does not claim real Mantis or private live-gateway coverage.

## Real behavior proof

target.title: fix(cron): don't classify a yielded isolated-cron turn as a fatal error
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an isolated-session scheduled (cron) agent run that ends by yielding — for example, after spawning subagents and pausing for them to complete — is reported as a fatal `error` and its delivery is suppressed, whenever a *non-fatal* tool error occurred earlier in the same turn (e.g. a shell `exec` that exits non-zero as benign control flow, like a `grep` with no match).

The run's actual work succeeds, but the schedule shows `error` / `consecutiveErrors` and no message is delivered.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveCronPayloadOutcome` only recognizes recovery from an earlier error via (a) a later successful payload or (b) a final assistant answer. A clean `sessions_yield` produces neither — a yielded turn emits no final assistant reply — so the earlier non-fatal error payload remains the de-facto terminal payload and drives `hasFatalStructuredErrorPayload = true`.

`sessions_yield` was never accounted for in the cron-outcome classifier; yield-awareness had previously been added only for media completions, not the textual/structured-payload path.

The fix threads the runner's existing `meta.yielded` flag into the classifier and treats a clean yield (no `runLevelError`, no fatal `failureSignal`) as a recovering, non-terminal outcome. A genuinely fatal `failureSignal`/`runLevelError` still flips the run fatal — yield-awareness does not mask real failures.

Non-goal: this does not re-deliver a digest assembled *after* spawned subagents finish (that path is a separate, deliberate short-circuit). Scope is strictly the misclassification of the yielded turn itself.

## User Impact

A scheduled isolated-agent run that legitimately yields is now reported as `ok` and its pre-yield output is delivered, instead of being marked failed with delivery suppressed. Operators stop seeing false `error` / `consecutiveErrors` on schedules that are actually working.

## Evidence

Two focused unit tests added to `src/cron/isolated-agent.helpers.test.ts`, written test-first (confirmed RED before the fix, GREEN after):

- `treats a clean sessions_yield as non-fatal despite an earlier benign tool error` — reproduces the bug: a benign `⚠️ 🛠️ … failed` payload before a clean yield no longer forces a fatal classification, and the successful pre-yield payload is preserved for delivery.
- `still marks a yielded turn fatal when a fatal failureSignal is present` — guard proving yield-awareness does not mask a genuinely fatal run.

```
 Test Files  108 passed (108)
      Tests  1144 passed (1144)
```
(full `vitest.cron` suite — no regressions; `oxlint` and `tsgo` core typecheck clean)

---
*Disclosure: prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); authored and reviewed by the submitter.*

## What Problem This Solves

Signal delivery targets are hard to reuse because DMs can be phone numbers or UUIDs, while groups use opaque group IDs. This adds OpenClaw-side Signal aliases so users can configure friendly names like `signal:me` or `signal:ops` once and use them in normal Signal delivery paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

The alias mapping belongs in the Signal plugin boundary because it is Signal-specific target normalization, not a cross-channel address book or Signal contact mutation. The implementation resolves config-backed aliases before outbound delivery, default target lookup, approval authorization/routing, directory listing, and outbound session route construction so Signal history and approval reactions use canonical Signal targets.

This intentionally does not mutate Signal contacts, discover live Signal contacts, or add wildcard/broad Signal access behavior. The only shared outbound change keeps directory-cache entries query-scoped so an exact alias lookup or miss cannot poison later peer/group resolution for Signal or sibling channel adapters.

## User Impact

Users can configure `channels.signal.aliases` or `channels.signal.accounts.<id>.aliases` with DM and group targets, then send to aliases such as `signal:ops`. Per-account aliases inherit top-level aliases and may override them. Invalid, blank, or recursive aliases fail before delivery with a clear Signal alias error.

target.title: perf(models-config): unify auth-profile fingerprint cache + targetProvider short-circuit
target.body:
## Summary

Improves `models.json` preparation so OpenClaw can skip expensive implicit-provider discovery when the relevant inputs are unchanged, while still re-planning when canonical auth state, plugin catalogs, or generated config inputs drift.

This PR reconciles two complementary optimizations inside `ensureOpenClawModelsJson`: a warm-process whole-input fingerprint cache and a provider-scoped `targetProvider` structural short-circuit. Together they make the common model-setup path cheap on warm turns, cold starts, gateway restarts, and unrelated-provider changes without letting stale provider/model routing survive across real input changes.

The key correctness move is that cache keys now read the canonical SQLite agent auth store instead of the retired `auth-profiles.json` file. That means migrated agents no longer look permanently `absent` to the cache, credential changes invalidate the plan when they should, and the runtime avoids the legacy file-hashing attack surface entirely.

## Why

`ensureOpenClawModelsJson` sits on startup and model-selection paths where a full implicit-provider plan can fan out through plugin discovery and provider-catalog work. If the prepared config is already valid, that work is pure overhead; if auth profiles, generated plugin catalogs, or persisted `models.json` inputs changed, reusing the old plan is a routing-integrity bug.

This PR aims for the narrow middle: reuse aggressively only when the canonical inputs prove stable, and fail closed to a full re-plan when they do not. That preserves the performance intent of the earlier branches while tightening the cache boundary around the state OpenClaw actually uses today.

## What Changed

- Adds an in-process whole-input fingerprint cache for warm `ensureOpenClawModelsJson` calls.
- Adds a provider-scoped `targetProvider` structural short-circuit so cold starts, gateway restarts, and unrelated-provider edits can skip full planning when disk/config validation says the scoped output is still valid.
- Fingerprints the canonical SQLite auth store (`openclaw-agent.sqlite`, via the warm pooled handle) instead of legacy `auth-profiles.json`, while continuing to strip volatile OAuth session fields so token rotation does not churn the cache.
- Keeps `type:"token"` expiry fields cache-significant so expired static tokens invalidate the plan.
- Threads generated plugin catalogs into the pre-plan parsed `models.json` and writes them consistently through skip, noop, and write paths.
- Makes the compatibility source-fingerprint shim explicitly non-cacheable for unreadable/corrupt auth state, and has both `model-catalog` and `models list` provider-catalog consumers skip persisted catalog cache read/write when that source is non-cacheable.
- Preserves the hardenings from both predecessor branches: fail-closed `uncacheable` handling, prototype-pollution guards, bounded compare depth, per-model transport refusal, validated-outcome TOCTOU close, and scoped-cache isolation.

## Relationship to Prior PRs

Supersedes #73260 and #73261 with one reconciled implementation. They were complementary, not redundant:

- **#73260** added content-hash auth-profile fingerprinting plus `models.json` drift detection. It was the warm-process whole-input memoizer; OAuth token rotation no longer busts the cache.
- **#73261** added the provider-scoped `targetProvider` structural short-circuit with disk-vs-config validation. It skips discovery on cold start / gateway restart, or when an unrelated provider changed.

Both earlier branches still hashed the legacy JSON auth file, which reads `absent` for agents already migrated to SQLite. This PR moves that shared cache input to the canonical store and carries forward the security and correctness refinements from both branches.

target.title: fix(memory-wiki): retry transient existing-page reads in wiki_apply and chatgpt import
target.body:
## Summary
Re-running `wiki_apply` `create_synthesis` for an existing synthesis page, or re-running the ChatGPT conversations import over already-imported pages, silently wipes the user's hand-written `## Notes` block and drops hand-added frontmatter when the existing-page read fails transiently (EBUSY/EMFILE/ENFILE style faults). The page is treated as brand-new and the regenerated content replaces the user's edits without any error surfacing.

PR #98360 fixed this defect class for `ingest.ts` and `source-page-shared.ts` (issue #98345) but did not cover these two surfaces.

## Root cause
Both surfaces swallow every existing-page read error and continue with an empty page.

Before, `extensions/memory-wiki/src/apply.ts:231` in `applyCreateSynthesisMutation`:

```ts
const existing = await root.readText(pagePath).catch(() => "");
```

Before, `extensions/memory-wiki/src/chatgpt-import.ts:762` in `importChatGptConversations`:

```ts
const existing = await fs.readFile(absolutePath, "utf8").catch(() => "");
```

With an empty `existing`, `applyCreateSynthesisMutation` keeps none of the frontmatter that only lived on disk (for example a hand-added `privacyTier`) and `buildSynthesisBody` regenerates an empty `## Notes` scaffold, which `writeWikiPage` then persists. In the importer, `preserveExistingPageBlocks` receives an empty `existing`, so the human notes and `## Related` blocks are not carried over, the write is misclassified as `create` instead of `update` or `skip`, and the rollback record snapshots an empty `existing` for that page.

## Fix
Route both reads through a local retry-once helper that treats only a genuinely missing page as new and propagates a failure that persists across the retry, the same shape #98360 shipped for ingest and imported-source pages. Unlike those two call sites, these reads have no existence gate (a missing page is the normal create path), so the helpers translate missing-page errors to an empty string instead of rethrowing them.

After, `extensions/memory-wiki/src/apply.ts`:

```ts
async function readExistingWikiPage(root: VaultRoot, pagePath: string): Promise<string> {
  try {
    return await root.readText(pagePath);
  } catch (error) {
    if (isMissingWikiPageError(error)) {
      return "";
    }
    try {
      return await root.readText(pagePath);
    } catch (retryError) {
      if (isMissingWikiPageError(retryError)) {
        return "";
      }
      throw retryError;
    }
  }
}
```

`isMissingWikiPageError` matches `FsSafeError` codes `not-found` and `path-alias`, the same missing-page classification `okf.ts` already uses for vault stat calls. `chatgpt-import.ts` gets the equivalent `readExistingConversationPage` keyed to plain `fs` `ENOENT`.

`writeWikiPage`'s change-detection read at `apply.ts:207` is routed through the same helper so the file has one canonical existing-page read; a transient failure there previously caused only a spurious identical rewrite, never data loss.

## Why this is the right boundary
- `apply.ts` owns the synthesis page lifecycle and `chatgpt-import.ts` owns imported conversation pages, so each gets the same local helper pattern #98360 established in `ingest.ts` and `source-page-shared.ts`, keyed to its own missing-page error shape (`FsSafeError` for the vault root, `ENOENT` for plain `fs`).
- These were the last two paths that merge preserved human content into a rewrite from a swallowed existing-page read. The remaining `.catch(() => "")` reads in the plugin are not user-content-lossy: `okf.ts:461` and `compile.ts:1377` use the read only for change detection before writing fully caller-computed content, and `okf.ts:496` fails safe by skipping removal.
- `compile.ts` `writeManagedMarkdownFile` and `writeDashboardPage` fall back to a fresh scaffold for plugin-generated index/dashboard/report pages; a transient read failure there can reset plugin-generated scaffolding but does not touch user-authored notes pages. Flagging as a candidate follow-up if the same retry treatment is wanted there.
- Fail-closed on persistent read errors matches the direction #98360 shipped: the mutation or import errors out and can be retried instead of silently destroying user edits.

## Verification
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-wiki/src/wiki-notes-read-retry.test.ts extensions/memory-wiki/src/apply.test.ts extensions/memory-wiki/src/import-runs.test.ts`: 3 files, 13 tests passed with the patch.
- The two new regression tests fail on pristine main 17482a4026 (notes and frontmatter wiped) and pass with the patch; the two pre-existing #98360 tests in the same suite stay green.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on the three changed files: clean.
- `oxfmt --check` on the three changed files: clean.
- `node scripts/run-tsgo.mjs -p tsconfig.extensions.json` and `-p test/tsconfig/tsconfig.extensions.test.json`: clean.

## Real behavior proof
Behavior addressed: a single transient read failure of the existing page during a create_synthesis re-run or a ChatGPT re-import silently empties the user's ## Notes block, drops hand-added frontmatter, and misclassifies the import operation.
Real environment tested: drove applyMemoryWikiMutation (the production wiki_apply mutation entry point) and importChatGptConversations (the production ChatGPT import entry point) against a real on-disk vault, on pristine main 17482a4026 and on the patched tree with identical inputs; vault initialization, markdown render/parse, compile, and all page writes were the real runtime on disk; the one injected fault was a single EBUSY error on the existing-page read.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: create the synthesis page via applyMemoryWikiMutation create_synthesis "Release Plan", hand-edit its notes block and add privacyTier frontmatter on disk, re-run the same mutation with one EBUSY injected on the syntheses/release-plan.md read; separately import a ChatGPT export via importChatGptConversations, hand-edit the conversation page notes, re-run the identical import with one EBUSY injected on that page read; then print the resulting page files.
Evidence after fix:
```
# BEFORE (pristine main 17482a4026)
$ wiki_apply create_synthesis 'Release Plan' (re-run with one EBUSY on the existing-page read)
syntheses/release-plan.md frontmatter privacyTier line: MISSING (hand-added frontmatter dropped)
syntheses/release-plan.md notes section:
## Notes
<!-- openclaw:human:start -->
<!-- openclaw:human:end -->

$ openclaw wiki chatgpt-import (re-run of same export with one EBUSY on the existing-page read)
import result: created=1 updated=0 skipped=0
chatgpt-2024-04-06-123456781234123412341234567890ab.md notes section:
## Notes
<!-- openclaw:human:start -->
<!-- openclaw:human:end -->

# AFTER (this patch, identical inputs)
$ wiki_apply create_synthesis 'Release Plan' (re-run with one EBUSY on the existing-page read)
syntheses/release-plan.md frontmatter privacyTier line: privacyTier: sensitive
syntheses/release-plan.md notes section:
## Notes
<!-- openclaw:human:start -->
Ship gate: legal sign-off required before GA.
<!-- openclaw:human:end -->

$ openclaw wiki chatgpt-import (re-run of same export with one EBUSY on the existing-page read)
import result: created=0 updated=0 skipped=1
chatgpt-2024-04-06-123456781234123412341234567890ab.md notes section:
## Notes
<!-- openclaw:human:start -->
HUMAN NOTE: verified against the airline booking.
<!-- openclaw:human:end -->
```
Observed result after fix: after one transient EBUSY on the existing-page read, the re-synthesized page keeps the user's notes line and hand-added privacyTier frontmatter, and the re-imported conversation page keeps its notes and is classified skipped instead of being recreated with an empty notes block.
What was not tested: no live gateway session drove wiki_apply over RPC; the EBUSY fault was injected at the read seam rather than produced by a real file lock; full build not run on this machine.

## Related
- #98345 reported this class for re-ingest; #98360 fixed `ingest.ts` and `source-page-shared.ts` only.
- #97523 covers the unsafe-local sync prune path and is unrelated to these read sites.
- Closed PRs #98364, #98367, #98555 all targeted the same two files as #98360 and do not touch `apply.ts` or `chatgpt-import.ts`.

Fixes #93043

## Verification

**Behavior addressed:** A user with a SecretRef-managed `gateway.auth.token` can explicitly recover the token for Control UI login without putting the bearer in terminal output, dashboard URLs, or browser-launch arguments.

**Real environment tested:** macOS host, local running OpenClaw Gateway on loopback, built CLI entry from this branch, temporary single-value file SecretRef provider for `gateway.auth.token`. Clipboard was restored after the proof.

## What Problem This Solves

`checks-node-core-tooling` can fail in the plugin lifecycle measure tests before the code under test is actually exercised. The Linux fixture reads temporary pid/ready files written by nested shell descendants. On a busy runner, the file path can be missing or still empty when the assertion reads it, and the `stubborn-descendant` fixture also used a 1s lifecycle timeout that can expire during nested process startup. The observed failure mode is `ENOENT` while reading `descendant.pid` in `test/scripts/plugin-lifecycle-measure.test.ts`.

This patch makes those fixtures wait for non-empty pid/ready files and gives the stubborn-descendant fixture enough startup budget while still verifying timeout cleanup and process-group termination.

## Summary

- wait for pid/ready fixture files to be non-empty before reading them in plugin lifecycle measure tests

target.title: fix(agents): bound model catalog JSON response reads for bedrock-mantle and huggingface
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Amazon Bedrock Mantle model discovery (`/v1/models`) and HuggingFace model discovery (`/models`) both parse successful HTTP responses with an unbounded `await response.json()`. On Node, `response.json()` buffers the entire body before parsing, so a provider-controlled endpoint can stream an arbitrarily large or never-ending JSON payload and push the discovery path into memory pressure, hangs, or OOM.

That matters here because both inputs are untrusted:

- Mantle discovery reads from an operator-selected AWS endpoint.
- HuggingFace discovery reads from an external router endpoint.

This PR closes the same response-body gap already fixed for sibling catalog surfaces in `#95418`, `#95420`, and `#96027`, but for the two remaining bundled provider discovery reads still using unbounded success-path JSON parsing on current `main`.

## Changes

- Replace the Mantle success-path read in `discoverMantleModels` with `readProviderJsonResponse(response, "bedrock-mantle.model-discovery")`.
- Replace the HuggingFace success-path read in `discoverHuggingfaceModels` with `readProviderJsonResponse(response, "huggingface.model-discovery")`.
- Reuse the existing shared provider JSON reader instead of introducing a new provider-local helper. That helper already enforces the standard 16 MiB JSON byte cap and wraps malformed JSON with a caller label.
- Preserve the existing fail-soft behavior around the changed call sites: Mantle still falls back to cached models or `[]` on discovery failure, and HuggingFace still falls back to the static bundled catalog on discovery failure.
- Update Mantle discovery tests to return real `Response` objects instead of plain `{ json() {} }` mocks so the changed path uses the same body/stream API shape as production.
- Add `scripts/proof-mantle-catalog-bound.mjs`, an affected-path proof harness that drives the real `discoverMantleModels` entry point against a local streaming server via injected `fetchFn`.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** a successful catalog response with no `Content-Length` must not be buffered whole if it exceeds the JSON safety cap; the read must stop near the cap, cancel the stream, and fail soft through the existing discovery fallback paths instead of draining the full body.
- **Affected entry point:** `discoverMantleModels` in `extensions/amazon-bedrock-mantle/discovery.ts` — the exact success-path function changed by this PR.
- **Real environment tested:** Node v22, local `node:http` server on `127.0.0.1`, streaming ~24 MiB catalog JSON in 64 KiB chunks with **no** `Content-Length`, injected via the production `fetchFn` parameter.
- **Exact proof shape:**
  1. Call `discoverMantleModels({ fetchFn })` against `/huge` → fail-soft fallback (`[]` when cache cold) plus early stream stop near the 16 MiB cap.
  2. Call against `/small` → normal catalog parses with model id intact.
  3. Warm cache from `/small`, expire refresh window, hit `/huge` → bounded overflow falls back to cached models.
- **Evidence after fix:**
  - Oversized stream: `discoverMantleModels` returned `[]` when cache was cold.
  - Early cancel: server sent **17,104,912 bytes**, near the 16 MiB cap rather than the full ~24 MiB body.
  - Happy path: small catalog parsed into exactly one model with id `anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6`.
  - Cached fallback: after warm cache + stale refresh, oversized stream returned the cached model instead of hanging or OOM.
- **Suite coverage:** `pnpm test extensions/amazon-bedrock-mantle/discovery.test.ts` passed **29/29** tests, including updated Mantle discovery tests that now use real `Response` objects on the success path.
- **HuggingFace note:** `discoverHuggingfaceModels` has no injectable fetch seam, but uses the same `readProviderJsonResponse` call-site pattern; Mantle affected-path proof exercises the bounded read + fail-soft catch path through the real changed discovery function.
- **What was not tested:** live Mantle or HuggingFace network endpoints; direct `discoverHuggingfaceModels` harness against a local streaming server.

## Evidence

```text
$ node --import tsx scripts/proof-mantle-catalog-bound.mjs

[case 1] discoverMantleModels + oversized /v1/models stream, no Content-Length
  ok: fail-soft fallback returns empty catalog when body exceeds cap — true
  ok: server stopped near 16 MiB cap, not full ~24 MiB (sent 17104912) — true
  ok: server did not stream the entire hostile body (sent 17104912 < 22649242) — true

[case 2] discoverMantleModels + normal small catalog still parses
  ok: small catalog returns one model — true
  ok: model id intact (anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6) — true

[case 3] discoverMantleModels uses cached models after oversized stream when cache warm
  ok: warm cache populated from small catalog — true
  ok: oversized stream falls back to cached models — true
  ok: cached model id preserved (anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-6) — true
  ok: stale refresh re-fetched before bounded overflow fallback — true

ALL PROOF ASSERTIONS PASSED
```

```text
$ pnpm test extensions/amazon-bedrock-mantle/discovery.test.ts -- --reporter=verbose

Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  29 passed (29)
```

**Label**: security

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(diagnostics): emit tool.execution.error for soft-error tool results
target.body:
Related: #55806

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators monitoring tool execution dashboards would see tools like `memory_search`, `composio_*`, `pages_*`, and `transcribe` reported as successful even when they returned error payloads (`status: unavailable`, `disabled: true`, `error: "…"`). The progress draft correctly showed these as failed (via `isToolResultError`), but OTEL/Prometheus telemetry counted them as `tool.execution.completed`, making error-rate dashboards unreliable.

## Why This Change Was Made

The diagnostic emit path in `wrapToolWithBeforeToolCallHook` only classified tool failures by caught exceptions (`catch` branch → `tool.execution.error`). Tools that return soft-error results without throwing were unconditionally emitted as `tool.execution.completed`. The stream observer already used `isToolResultError(result)` from `tool-result-error.ts` to detect these — this change reuses the same predicate in the telemetry emit path so both classifications agree.

The `errorCategory` is derived from `readToolResultStatus(result)` (the normalized `details.status` string, e.g. `"unavailable"`, `"disabled"`, `"timeout"`), falling back to `"ToolReportedError"` when no status is present but other error signals match (`ok: false`, `Boolean(details.error)`, non-zero `exitCode`).

## User Impact

Tool execution error dashboards (Grafana/Prometheus panels filtering on `openclaw_errorCategory != ""`) will now correctly surface soft-error tool calls. No change to agent behavior or user-facing tool output — only the diagnostic telemetry classification changes.

## Evidence

- New test: `"emits tool.execution.error when execute returns a soft-error result without throwing"` — mocks a tool returning `{ details: { status: "unavailable", disabled: true, error: "…" } }` and asserts that the emitted event is `tool.execution.error` with `errorCategory: "unavailable"` (not `tool.execution.completed`).
- All 59 existing tests in `agent-tools.before-tool-call.e2e.test.ts` continue to pass.
- `pnpm test src/agents/agent-tools.before-tool-call.e2e.test.ts` — 59 passed, 0 failed.

🤖 AI-assisted (Claude Code). I understand the change and have verified it locally.

target.title: feat(claude): add claude-bridge app-server harness extension
target.body:
## Summary

TL;DR:
Inspiration: https://openclaw.ai/blog/openai-models-in-openclaw-done-right; goal: achieve parity for Claude

New feature; issue https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/93793

OpenClaw currently has no first-class harness for Anthropic models. Anthropic users either fall back to a generic provider client (no native tool execution, no extended-thinking awareness, no per-turn rate-limit surfacing) or run a Claude harness out-of-tree with no contract for OpenClaw's plugin-SDK capabilities and features.

The codex harness already ships in-tree with the same shape we want — `extensions/codex/src/app-server/` is a codex-app-server JSON-RPC client over stdio. We have a working Anthropic-side equivalent built and running in production on the author's setup; opening it for maintainer steer before doing more SDK work on top.

Harness: this PR
JSON-RPC server: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@zeroaltitude/openclaw-claude-bridge

**What is the intended outcome?**

- Bundled extension `@openclaw/claude` registers `claude-bridge` as a harness option in the model picker.
- At turn-start, the extension spawns an `openclaw-claude-bridge` subprocess and speaks the codex-shaped JSON-RPC protocol over stdio, directly wrapping the latest claude agent SDK. The server (currently published as `@zeroaltitude/openclaw-claude-bridge`  https://www.npmjs.com/package/@zeroaltitude/openclaw-claude-bridge — fork-preview path; would migrate to `@openclaw/openclaw-claude-bridge` if the maintainers republish it) handles Anthropic API I/O, rate-limit surfacing, image-payload sanitization, and plugin-thread-config persistence.
- Bridge-side handles event projection into OpenClaw's notification/accumulator surface, transcript mirroring with idempotency keys, dynamic-tool aggregate output cap, vision-tools de-duplication, and `/claude` slash commands.
- See `extensions/claude/README.md` for the full feature map.

**What is intentionally out of scope?**

- Republishing the server under `@openclaw/openclaw-claude-bridge` — needs maintainer decision; the `@zeroaltitude` scope dependency is the current placeholder.
- Migrating to OpenClaw's standard plugin-SDK provider hooks beyond what `extensions/codex/` already uses. The bridge follows codex's pattern verbatim where applicable.
- Anything outside the harness bridge surface.

**What does success look like?** Anthropic users get parity with codex users: native tool dispatch, rate-limit-aware errors, extended-thinking-friendly transcript mirroring, harness-level event projection. No regressions to existing harnesses.

**What should reviewers focus on?**

1. **Scope concern — am I taking too much core?** The branch touches `src/plugins/command-registration.ts`, `src/plugins/current-plugin-metadata-snapshot.ts`, `src/plugins/agent-tool-result-middleware-types.ts`, `src/auto-reply/reply/get-reply-native-slash-fast-path.ts`, `src/agents/model-runtime-aliases.ts`, and `src/agents/tools/image-tool.ts`. Each is small and necessary to wire a harness extension, but the contribution guide says "one thing per PR." Happy to split into prep PRs first if maintainers prefer.
2. **External-plugin vs. bundled-extension** — Per CONTRIBUTING.md "most features should be third-party plugins." Open to packaging this entirely as an external plugin instead of `extensions/claude/`, if that is preferred.
3. **Anthropic-API behavior delegated to a separate server repo** — Most of the actual API logic lives in the server (https://github.com/zeroaltitude/openclaw-plugins/tree/main/openclaw-claude/server -- https://www.npmjs.com/package/@zeroaltitude/openclaw-claude-bridge). Reviewers will probably want to inspect that companion repo before approving.
4. **`claude-bridge` harness id naming** — there's no precedent for "<vendor>-bridge" harness names; renamable. (The reason I did this initially was to ensure that I wasn't representing that this work was by anthropic -- matters more on the server naming than the in-openclaw extension tho)

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** Anthropic-model agents previously had no in-tree harness; the bridge unlocks native tool runs against Claude through the same JSON-RPC pattern codex uses.
- **Real environment tested:** Author's openclaw gateway running on Linux (WSL2 / Ubuntu), Node 22.x. Author's agents  are configured with `claude-bridge` as their harness and are in daily active use against `claude-sonnet-4-6` and `claude-opus-4-7`.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**
  1. `pnpm install && pnpm build`
  2. `openclaw gateway restart --deep`
  3. Send a Slack DM to one of the claude-bridge agents
  4. Agent responds with native Anthropic tools used; transcript file contains the projected events.
  5. `/claude status` in the same thread prints shared-client liveness.
- **Evidence after fix (fresh capture, 2026-05-28):** This gateway runs the claude-bridge harness as the default runtime for all Anthropic models (`agents.defaults.models.*.agentRuntime.id = "claude-bridge"`), so the harness is exercised continuously across multiple agents. Captured live:
  1. **Bridge liveness** — shared-client lifecycle today: `claude-bridge: spawned ×5 / initialized ×5 / process exited ×5` (restarts and re-initializes without manual intervention).
  2. **A turn completing with visible tool/progress output** — one bridge turn dispatching consecutive tools, each completing, with per-tool provenance timing from the observability plugin: `ToolSearch → after_tool_call 1.9ms`, `exec → 1.7ms`, `Write → 1.9ms`, `Agent → 1.9ms`.
  3. **Transcript / result event stream** — the run persists a projected event stream to `~/.openclaw/agents/<id>/sessions/<uuid>.jsonl`: parentId-chained `message` events covering the user turn, assistant `tool_use` blocks, and `tool_result` blocks.
  4. **`/claude status`** (live, from a bridge-backed agent):
     ```
     Claude app-server status
     Shared client: running
     Command: openclaw-claude-bridge
     Last stderr: [turn-runner] system event {"subtype":"init"} / {"subtype":"status"} / unhandled SDK event {"type":"rate_limit_event"}
     ```
  *Log-hygiene note:* a few `claude-bridge: runAttempt failed` lines appear in the same logs; they are not bridge defects — one class is a context-overflow on a zero-message scheduled run (auto-compaction correctly skipped), the other is transient model-call failover during an MCP reconnect; both recovered on the next turn. Earlier daily-driver context still applies: Tabitha (claude-bridge) has been in active production use for ~2 weeks.
- **Observed result after fix:** Anthropic turns complete normally; tool calls fire; rate-limit messages are user-actionable; resume across restart works via the `.claude-binding.json` sidecar.
- **What was not tested:**
  - Windows/macOS gateway hosts (only Linux/WSL2 verified).
  - Bun runtime (Node 22 only).
  - Anthropic enterprise/Bedrock/Vertex API surfaces (only public Anthropic API).
  - Concurrent multi-account scenarios beyond 3 agents.
- **Proof limitations or environment constraints:** Author runs a single-host gateway. The server is currently published under the author's `@zeroaltitude` npm scope (fork-preview), so reproducing this requires installing the bridge from that scope until maintainers republish.
- **Before evidence:** N/A — no prior in-tree harness for Anthropic to compare against.

## Tests and validation

- Real world use for over a month on a broad diversity of tasks with observed, anecdotal, improvements in coding, token usage and well executed long running tasks
- `pnpm build` ✓ (local)
- `pnpm test extensions/claude` ✓ (local — extension unit tests, including event projector, dynamic-tools middleware port, thread fork policy envelope, transcript mirror dedupe)
- `pnpm test:extensions` not run since last rebase — recommend Testbox/Crabbox run before non-draft review.
- No `CHANGELOG.md` edit per contributor rule; maintainer to add on land.

## Risk checklist

- **Did user-visible behavior change?** Yes — new `claude-bridge` harness appears in model picker; new `/claude` slash command surface.
- **Did config, environment, or migration behavior change?** Yes — new plugin `configSchema` (see `extensions/claude/openclaw.plugin.json`). Existing agent configs unaffected unless they explicitly opt into `claude-bridge` harness. Doctor contract added (`extensions/claude/doctor-contract-api.ts`).
- **Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change?** Yes (intentional). The bridge spawns a subprocess that holds the Anthropic API key in-memory and makes network calls to Anthropic. Subprocess lifecycle is owned by the harness, not user shell. The plugin SDK enabler changes (e.g. `command-registration.ts`) are additive and follow existing codex-extension precedent.
- **Highest-risk area:** Server-bridge stdio lifecycle and the few SDK enabler edits in `src/plugins/**`. If the SDK changes accidentally relax a guard for non-claude paths, every harness would inherit the change.
- **How is that risk mitigated?** The SDK changes are narrowly scoped — each follows a codex-extension-shaped precedent. Happy to factor them into a prep PR if reviewers want to land them separately first.

## Current review state

- **Next action:** Maintainer steer on scope: (a) accept as bundled extension as-is, (b) split SDK enablers into a prep PR first, or (c) request packaging as an external plugin.
- **Still waiting on:** Maintainer decision on the above. CI run on this push.
- **Bot/reviewer comments addressed:** None yet — opening draft.

---

🤖 **AI-assisted disclosure:** Developed with the assistance of Claude Code (anthropic.com/claude-code). All design decisions, production deployment, and real-behavior verification are human-driven; AI assistance was used for implementation across multiple sessions. Session transcripts available on request.

target.title: fix(memory): keep shared QMD manager alive on active-memory recall timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes #96455. After an `active-memory` embedded recall run times out, chat-session `memory_search` returns `"memory search manager is closed"` even though `openclaw memory search --agent main` keeps working against the same QMD backend. The first closed-manager result can also trip the 60s `memory_search` cooldown, so recovery looks sticky until the gateway restarts.

Root cause: active-memory's recall-timeout cleanup (`scheduleMemorySearchCleanupAfterTimeout`) called `closeActiveMemorySearchManager`, which fully retired the **agent-scoped shared QMD manager** that chat `memory_search` and the startup timers/watchers depend on. A request-scoped recall timeout was tearing down long-lived shared state.

## Why This Change Was Made

The cleanup's legitimate job (introduced in #84048) is to release the **disposable local builtin index/embedding providers** a hung recall can leave open — not to retire the shared manager. The fix keeps the shipped close contract intact and does not grow the SDK surface:

- `closeActiveMemorySearchManager` gains a backward-compatible optional `scope?: "manager" | "index-managers"`. Default `"manager"` is the unchanged full-close behavior. `"index-managers"` releases **only** the disposable local index managers (a narrow `releaseMemoryIndexManagers` path in memory-core) and leaves the shared QMD manager alive.
- active-memory's recall-timeout cleanup now calls `closeActiveMemorySearchManager({ ..., scope: "index-managers" })`.
- No new public SDK export is added (the public callable export count is unchanged), so the prior review's `merge-risk: compatibility` (expanded plugin-facing API surface) no longer applies.

The recall's own in-flight QMD query is already cancelled via the embedded run abort signal, so the preserved manager stays healthy — it is the same long-lived manager CLI search and startup timers use successfully.

Addresses the prior review:
- **Compatibility / API surface:** reworked from a new SDK facade to a backward-compatible optional param — no export-count growth.
- **P1 (active-memory timeout test):** the timeout-cleanup test now asserts the `scope: "index-managers"` call, proving the new path.
- **P2 (absent release hook):** intentional no-op with a documenting comment — falling back to full-close would reintroduce #96455.

## User Impact

Users with `active-memory` enabled and a QMD-backed `memory_search` no longer lose chat memory recall after an active-memory recall timeout. The disposable local index/embedding cleanup from #84048 is preserved; only the over-broad shared-manager teardown is removed. No config or API removal; one additive optional param on an existing facade.

## Evidence

Reworked on latest `upstream/main`. Single commit; +134 / -11 across 13 files; SDK callable-export surface unchanged.

### Real QMD-backed runtime proof (qmd 2.5.3)

Installed real `@tobilu/qmd` 2.5.3 (BM25 `searchMode: "search"`). Drove the **real, un-mocked** memory-core `FallbackMemoryManager` (QMD-backed) through the recall-timeout cleanup path vs the full close:

```
[proof] manager#1: FallbackMemoryManager error: (none)
[proof] BEFORE cleanup: search outcome: {"ok":true,"hits":0}
[proof] AFTER releaseMemoryIndexManagers: sameManager: true
[proof] AFTER cleanup: search outcome: {"ok":true,"hits":0}
[proof] AFTER full close: old-manager search outcome: {"ok":false,"message":"memory search manager is closed"}
[proof] after close, fresh get is new manager: true
```

- After the recall-timeout release path: the **same** shared manager is preserved and `search` stays usable — no `"memory search manager is closed"`.
- After a full close (the old behavior): the manager throws exactly `"memory search manager is closed"` — the issue's literal symptom — and a fresh manager is created.

Real qmd BM25 retrieval is healthy on the manager's own index (the `hits:0` above is a separate qmd multi-collection/BM25-scoring nuance on the manager's filtered CLI path, unrelated to manager liveness):

```
$ qmd search "Falcon launch"   # against the manager's own index.sqlite
qmd://memory-root-main/MEMORY.md:3 #e5bc2f
Title: Memory

Project Falcon launch window opens in March. The methalox engine passed static fire.
```

### Regression tests

```
extensions/memory-core/src/memory/search-manager.test.ts ... 37 passed
src/plugins/memory-runtime.test.ts ........................ 12 passed (incl. scope-routing)
src/plugin-sdk/memory-host-search.test.ts ................. 4 passed  (incl. scope passthrough)
extensions/active-memory/index.test.ts ................... 152 passed (timeout asserts scope)
test/scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.test.ts ............. 7 passed  (callable-export budget unchanged)
```

- `memory-runtime.test.ts`: routes `scope: "index-managers"` to the release path without retiring the shared manager.

### Local validation

